summary: Sets out requirements for a service that lets users prove data existed at a given time and has not been changed since, even over very long periods. It also covers verifying signatures after long gaps. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Files and signatures do not last as long as the claims people make about them. This memo describes a service that keeps data safe for decades, keeps the proof that it has not changed, and can still check a signature made years ago.

questions: what is a long term archive service
subtitle: What a digital archive must do to keep data, and proof of its integrity, for decades.

tldr.problem: Digital data does not keep its promises on its own: a file can outlive the format and medium that store it, and a signed document can outlive both the certificate used to check it and the algorithm that produced it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a class of long-term archive service and states seven groups of technical requirements for it, covering submission, retrieval and deletion, a written archive policy, management of archived objects, evidence records that show data was not altered, confidentiality, transfer between providers, and groups of related objects.
tldr.outcome: The document is a requirements statement rather than a protocol, so it defines nothing that later replaced it. It is informational and has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Evidence record may contain
facts.value: Acknowledgements, time stamps, certificates, revocation information, trust anchors and policy details

today: RFC 4810 is an Informational document published in March 2007, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements rather than defining a protocol, so nothing in it has been superseded. It points at RFC 3161 for the time-stamp protocol it assumes.

sections.title: Why Long-Term Archives Are Needed
sections.content:
Digital data does not keep its promises on its own. A file's useful life can outlast the format and the storage medium that hold it. A signed document can outlive the certificate used to check the signature, and it can outlive the algorithm that made the signature, which is the point after which that algorithm no longer gives the protection it was designed to give.

A long-term archive service preserves data over long periods through technical and procedural routines, such as refreshing time stamps and moving data to new storage media, so that a claim about the data can still be made in the future. The service can supply evidence that a document existed at a particular time and has not changed since, and it can let signatures be checked years after they were made. The archive may sit inside an organisation's own network or run as an external service reached over the Internet, and it may use time stamping from independent providers.

The RFC lists the kinds of claim the service must support: wills, land records, medical data, criminal case files, personnel files and contracts. Submitters include companies storing contracts with a third party, hospitals storing medical data on an internal service, individuals who want evidence of possessing data at a particular time, and law enforcement officers who need to show integrity years later. In each case there is a matching retriever, such as a company retrieving a contract during a dispute or an officer preparing a criminal trial.
sections.plainLanguage: Files and signatures do not last as long as the claims people make about them. This memo describes a service that keeps data safe for decades and keeps the proof that it has not changed.

sections.title: Who Is Involved and What Is Preserved
sections.content:
The RFC borrows the archiving community's vocabulary so that requirements can be stated precisely. A submitter hands data to the archive and a retriever later asks for it back. The originator produced the data and may have signed it, but need not know the archive or its records. An arbitrator is the party who must be satisfied that the data's origin, integrity or time of existence is genuine. A modifier changes attributes attached to an archived object or its evidence record.

The data itself is an archived data object, and the period during which it is kept is the archival period. An archive package holds archived data objects together with the evidence record collected for them. An evidence record may include the archive's acknowledgements, time stamps and verification data such as public-key certificates, revocation information, trust anchors, policy details and role information. A time stamp is an attestation from a Time Stamping Authority that a data item existed at a certain time.

Two sets of rules govern the service. The long-term archive policy defines the operational characteristics of the service. The cryptographic maintenance policy defines how to maintain the validity of digitally signed objects if a hash or signature algorithm becomes weak, or if one of the private keys used to create a signature is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names the people involved: the one who hands data over, the one who made it, the one who asks for it later, and the one who has to be convinced the data is genuine. It also names the things: the stored data, its evidence record, and the rules the archive works under.

sections.title: Basic Operations, Policy and Management
sections.content:
Clients must be able to submit data objects for archiving, retrieve them, and delete them. After a submission the service must return an identifier that can be used to fetch the data or its evidence, for example a hash value of the object, although holding that value is not automatically permission to see the data. Requests and responses must be authenticatable, an authorization policy must be defined and observed, and the archive may refuse deletion as a matter of policy. A deposit must be acknowledged so the submitter can confirm the right data was accepted, and a generic query mechanism is needed so that an acknowledgement can be delayed by a grace period without leaving the submitter in doubt.

The service must operate under a long-term archive policy with three parts: an archived data object maintenance policy, an authorization policy and a service policy. The maintenance policy should cover preservation activity triggers, the default archival period and the default handling when that period expires. Policies must be unambiguously identified, for example by an object identifier, and the service must be able to say which policies apply to a given archived object.

Management of archived objects must also be possible. Clients must be able to set, extend or shorten the archival period, which may be expressed in terms of time, an event, or both. They must be able to attach metadata such as classification codes, type of format, contributors, title, author and date. They must be able to choose the policy the data is handled under, and the service must report the policy it enforces and return an error when it cannot support the one requested.

Appendix A sketches four shapes the service can take: one that stores data for authenticated users and gives evidence supporting non-repudiation; a pure non-repudiation service that only generates time stamps and verification data and does not retrieve or delete anything; a service run inside an organisation's own network, which should take its non-repudiation evidence from a third party because an internally generated acknowledgement may be viewed as worthless; and an external service offered over the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The archive must let clients put data in, take it out and delete it. It must work under a written policy, let clients say how long to keep each item and attach labels to it, and tell clients which policy it actually applied.

sections.title: Evidence Records, Confidentiality and Groups
sections.content:
The service must be able to provide evidence that demonstrates the integrity of the data it holds, from the moment it received the data until the archival period expires. This may take the form of evidence records supporting long-term non-repudiation of the data's existence at a point in time, as in a legal dispute. The record should carry enough information for an arbitrator to be shown the relevant characteristics, though those vary: authenticating the originator is not always possible, for example when the submitted object is unsigned or lacks the information needed to check the signer. Evidence records must be structured so that modifications to the data or to the record can be detected, including modifications made by the archive's own administrators.

An archive need not supply every piece of evidence a non-repudiation proof would need, and in some cases should not be trusted to. Trust anchors and algorithm security policies are better provided by other services, since an archive that supplied the trust anchors could forge a record that those anchors would verify. Confidentiality must be supported, including between submitter and archive, and the service must accept encrypted data in a way that later preservation work still applies to the original, unencrypted data. Encryption must not put the evidence record at risk, and contact information for the parties responsible for each object should be kept so warning messages can be sent when encryption algorithms need maintenance.

Data and evidence must be transferable from one service to another, so an archive can close before an archival period ends and a submitter can change provider. Evidence records must be able to span several providers over time without losing their value. The service should also handle groups of objects: submitters should be able to say which objects belong together, retrievers should be able to take one, some or all of them, and a single evidence record should be able to cover a document and its signature file. Non-repudiation proof must still be available for each object separately.
sections.plainLanguage: The heart of the service is the evidence record: proof that the stored data has not changed since the day it arrived. The archive keeps that proof so carefully that even its own administrators cannot quietly alter it, and it lets clients keep their data private while still doing the maintenance work.

sections.title: Operational and Legal Considerations
sections.content:
An archive has to work efficiently even when it holds a great many archived objects. To limit expense and keep up performance it should minimise the use of trusted third parties, so that the design limits the number of time stamps needed to provide the desired level of service. Necessity of access to archived objects should also be minimised: an object may only need to be opened when a user requests it, or when the hash algorithms used for indexing or for evidence record generation become insecure.

Legal rules constrain the service as well. An archive must be able to operate under any applicable legal regime. For example, it may have to reject a deletion request from an otherwise authorised requestor when the target of the request has been subpoenaed by law enforcement authorities. Some applications need to process a chain of archive policies present in an evidence record, for example to ensure that compatible policies were used throughout the lifetime of the archived data objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping a lot of data for a long time costs money, so the archive should use outside helpers sparingly and only open a stored file when it really must. Legal orders can also stop it from deleting something a client has asked it to remove.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Data is the principal asset that a long-term archive service protects, and the principal threat is an undetected loss of data integrity. Where signature verification relies on a public key infrastructure, certificate revocation can retroactively invalidate signatures that were valid before. An archive may support a claim made by an alleged signer by collecting revocation information after a grace period during which a compromise can be reported, or by preserving subsequent revocation information.

Access control choices must account for the lifespan of the archived object: the credentials of the entity that submitted data may no longer be available or valid when the data is finally retrieved. Formats also stop being supported over time, and the software needed to process content or check signatures may no longer be available. This is a particular problem with non-standard formats or proprietary processing, so the submitter should take care to avoid it, for example by periodically retrieving the data, converting it and re-submitting it in a new format. Additional mechanisms, applications or tools may then be needed to preserve the value of the evidence records attached to the original object.

A long-term archive system may also have to correlate different identities that represent the same entity at different points in time, for example an individual recorded under different employers at different times. Maintenance activities must run on a schedule that weighs the strength of the relevant cryptographic algorithms, the lifespan of the relevant certification authorities, and the revocation status of relevant entities such as time stamping authorities. Standards for the use of cryptographic algorithms are expected to be established by organisations or governmental bodies, not by individual archive services.
sections.plainLanguage: The danger is that stored data quietly changes and nobody notices. The memo also warns that old certificates, old keys and old file formats can all expire while the data is still needed, so the archive must keep checking, refreshing and re-recording.
